title: 是: A is B
why: 是 links two nouns: A is B. It never changes, so there is no am, are, is, was or were to choose between.
mistake: 是 joins nouns. Don't put it in front of a describing word like 高 (see 很).

title: 不 and 没: saying no
pattern: 不 + verb (isn't, won't, doesn't) · 没 + verb (didn't, hasn't)
why: 不 says something isn't so, or that someone doesn't or won't do it. 没 says something didn't happen. 有 always takes 没.
mistake: 有 is the one verb that never takes 不.
gap: She isn't going to school tomorrow.

title: 吗: yes-or-no questions
why: Put 吗 on the end of a statement and it becomes a yes-or-no question. The word order stays exactly the same.
mistake: A question word like 什么 already makes a question, so it doesn't need 吗.
gap: Are you going to school today?

title: 的: my, and describing
why: The owner or the description always comes before the thing, the opposite of "the book of mine". With close family it is often dropped: 我妈妈.
mistake: Owner first, then 的, then the thing.
order: My friend's home is very big.

title: Measure words
pattern: Number or 这/那 + measure word + noun
why: A number can't sit directly on a noun: a measure word goes between them. 个 is the general one, 本 is for books, 杯 for cups and 只 for many animals. For "two" of something, say 两, not 二.
mistake: A number needs a measure word before the noun.
ex: I'd like two cups of tea.
gap: There are three books on the table.
I'd like a glass of water.
There are five people in our family.
order: She wants three cups of coffee.

title: 很 + describing word
why: Chinese adjectives work like verbs, so they don't need 是. 很 usually joins them, and often means little more than "is", not a strong "very".
order: My mum is very busy today.

title: 也 and 都: too and all
pattern: Subject + 也 or 都 + verb
why: Both go straight before the verb, never at the front of the sentence. 都 sums up the people or things named before it.
mistake: 也 follows the subject and comes before the verb.
gap: She likes cats, and I like cats too.
We are all going to school.
order: My friend is also a teacher.

title: 在 + place + verb
why: Where something happens comes before the action: literally "I at home eat". English puts it at the end.
mistake: The place goes before the verb.
gap: My mum works at a hospital.

title: Time goes before the verb
pattern: Time + subject + verb, or subject + time + verb
why: When something happens goes before the verb, either at the very start of the sentence or just after the subject. It doesn't go at the end, as it can in English.
mistake: The time word comes before the verb.
ex: I am going to Beijing tomorrow.
gap: I am going to school tomorrow.
order: I go to school every day.
My dad works in the morning.
I am not going to Beijing this year.
spot: I am going to school tomorrow.

title: 了 after a verb: it's done
why: 了 after a verb says the action was completed. It isn't a past tense: it marks that something got done, and it usually comes with an amount, as in 三本书. To say it didn't happen, use 没 and drop the 了.
mistake: 没 already says it didn't happen, so 了 goes.
ex: He drank a cup of tea.
She ate a lot of apples.
gap: I bought two cups of coffee.
She drank a glass of water.
order: We drank three cups of tea.

title: 有: have, and there is
pattern: Person + 有 + thing · Place + 有 + thing
why: 有 means "have", and after a place it means "there is". Its negative is always 没有.
mistake: For "there is", use 有, not 是.
ex: There is a book on the table.
There are many students in the school.
gap: There is a cat at home.
order: There are three people at home.
spot: There are many people in the classroom.
I don't have an older brother.

title: 在: is at a place
why: 是 says what something is. 在 says where it is, and it is the verb of the sentence, so no 是 is needed.
mistake: He isn't a school: use 在 for where someone is.
ex: The book is on the table.
gap: My phone is on the table.
order: The cat is on the table.
spot: The book is on the table.

title: 呢: and you?
why: 呢 after a person or thing asks the same question about them, or asks where they are. It saves repeating yourself.
mistake: 吗 needs a whole statement before it. For "and you?", use 呢.
ex: I'm having tea, what about him?
gap: He is going to Beijing, and you?

title: Question words stay in place
pattern: The question word goes where the answer will go
why: English moves "what" and "where" to the front. Chinese leaves them where the answer would be, so a question has the same order as its answer.

title: 几 and 多少: how many
pattern: 几 + measure word + noun · 多少 + noun
why: 几 is for numbers you expect to be small, and it needs a measure word. 多少 is for any amount, and often goes straight on the noun, as in 多少钱.
mistake: 几 needs a measure word, just as a number does.
ex: How many children do you have?
gap: How many people are in your family?
What day of the week is it today?
order: How many books do you have?
How much is this cup of tea?
spot: How many books do you have?

title: 会: can, a skill you learned
why: 会 is for what you have learned to do: speak a language, drive, swim. It goes before the verb.
mistake: 会, then the verb, then what you do.

title: 想: would like to
why: 想 before a verb says what you would like to do. It is softer than 要. 不想 goes in front for "don't want to".
ex: He wants to go to China.
gap: I'd like to go to Beijing.
What would you like to eat?
order: I'd like to buy a book.
We want to go to school tomorrow.
spot: He wants to eat an apple.

title: 能: can, if it's possible
why: 能 says that something is possible or allowed. 会 is for a skill you have learned; 能 is for whether you are able to right now.
mistake: 吗 goes at the very end.

title: 和: and, between nouns
why: 和 joins people and things. Unlike English "and", it doesn't join verbs or whole sentences.
ex: Dad and Mum are both busy.
gap: You and I are both students.
Dad and Mum are at home.
order: The teachers and students are all at school.

title: 太…了: too, or so
why: 太…了 means "too" or, when you are pleased, "so". The 了 here has nothing to do with the past. 不太 means "not very", and takes no 了.
mistake: No 是, and finish with 了.

title: 吧: let's, and right?
why: 吧 softens a sentence into a suggestion ("let's"), or turns it into a guess you want confirmed ("right?").
mistake: 吧 goes at the very end.

title: 要: going to, want
why: 要 before a verb says you are going to do something, or firmly want to. It is stronger than 想.
ex: I am going to Beijing tomorrow.
What do you want to buy?
gap: I want to buy a book.
He is going to school tomorrow.
What do you want to drink?
order: What do you want to buy?
spot: I am going to school tomorrow.
What do you want to drink?

title: 正在: doing it right now
why: 正在 before a verb says the action is going on right now. 在 alone can do the same, and 呢 often ends the sentence.
mistake: 正在 means it is still going on, so it doesn't take 了.

title: 过: have you ever
why: 过 after a verb says you have done it at some time in your life. To say you never have, use 没, and keep the 过.
mistake: 过 takes 没, not 不.
ex: Have you ever had Chinese food?
gap: I have never been to Beijing.
order: Have you ever had Chinese food?
spot: I have never been to China.

title: 比: more than
why: 比 compares two things, and the adjective alone already means "more". That is why 很 can't go with it.
mistake: No 很 in a 比 sentence.
ex: This book is more expensive than that one.
gap: This one is bigger than that one.
order: This book is more expensive than that book.

title: 跟…一样: the same as
why: 跟…一样 says two things are the same. Add an adjective to say in what way: as tall as, as cold as.
mistake: No 很 before the adjective here.
ex: I am as tall as him.
This is the same as that.
Today is as cold as yesterday.
gap: I am as tall as him.
This is the same as that.
Today is as hot as yesterday.
order: I am as tall as her.
This book is the same as that book.
Today is as cold as yesterday.
spot: I am as tall as him.
This is the same as that.

title: 得: how something is done
why: 得 after a verb describes how well or how fast it is done. If there is an object, it goes first: 他中文说得很好.
mistake: The object can't come straight after 得.

title: 给: for, or to someone
why: 给 before a person says who the action is for or to. As a verb on its own, it simply means "give".
mistake: The person goes straight after 给.
ex: The teacher gives us a book.
gap: He bought me a cup of tea.
Please give me a glass of water.
order: Please give me a cup of tea.

title: 从…到: from and to
why: 从 marks where or when something starts, 到 where or when it ends. The whole phrase goes before the verb.
mistake: 从 and its place come before the verb.
ex: It is close from my home to the school.
I work from eight to five.
gap: They go from Shanghai to Beijing.
order: It is close from my home to the school.
I work from eight to five.
spot: It is far from here to there.

title: 离: how far from
pattern: A + 离 + B + 远 or 近
why: 离 says how far apart two places are, or two times. English says "from" here, but 从 won't do: 从 is for moving, 离 for distance.
ex: My home is close to the school.
It isn't far from here to the hospital.
gap: My home is close to the school.
It is far from here to Beijing.
The school isn't far from my home.
order: My home is close to the school.
The hospital isn't far from here.
spot: My home is close to the school.
It is far from here to Beijing.

title: 因为…所以: because, so
why: Chinese often marks both halves: the reason with 因为, the result with 所以. In English you would use only one of them.
mistake: The reason comes first, with 因为.
ex: Because it's raining, I'm not going.
He is busy, so he didn't come.
因为我喜欢中国，所以学中文。
I like China, so I study Chinese.
gap: Because it's cold today, I'm not going.
He is ill, so he didn't come to school.
It's too expensive, so I'm not buying it.
order: Because it's raining, I'm not going.
He is too busy, so he didn't come.
Because it's cold, I'm not going.
spot: Because it's raining, I'm not going.
I was busy, so I didn't come.

title: 虽然…但是: although, but
pattern: 虽然 + one thing，但是 + the other
why: Saying "although … but" is wrong in English, and right in Chinese. Both halves are normally marked.
mistake: 虽然 pairs with 但是, not 所以.
ex: It's expensive, but I want to buy it.
Although it was raining, he came.
虽然很累，但是我很高兴。
gap: It's expensive, but I want to buy it.
He is busy, but he came.
order: 虽然|很|累|，|但是|我|很|高兴|。
Although it was raining, he came.
It's expensive, but I want to buy it.
spot: It's expensive, but I want to buy it.

title: 还是 and 或者: or
pattern: Question: A 还是 B？ · Statement: A 或者 B
why: Chinese has two words for "or". 还是 asks which one. 或者 says either one will do.
mistake: When you are asking which, use 还是.
ex: Are you having tea or coffee?
Are you going today or tomorrow?
Tea or coffee, either is fine.
gap: Are you having tea or coffee?
Is he a teacher or a student?
Today or tomorrow, either is fine.
order: Are you having tea or coffee?
Is he a teacher or a student?
Are you going today or tomorrow?
spot: Are you having tea or coffee?

title: 已经…了: already
why: 已经 means "already", and the sentence normally ends in 了, to say that this is now how things stand.

title: 有点儿 and 一点儿: a bit
pattern: 有点儿 + adjective · adjective + 一点儿
why: 有点儿 goes before the adjective, and usually sounds like a complaint: a bit too cold. 一点儿 goes after it, and compares or asks for a change: a bit cheaper.
mistake: Before an adjective, use 有点儿.
order: This book is a bit expensive.

title: 先…然后: first, then
pattern: 先 + first thing，然后 + next thing
why: 先 goes before the first verb, after the subject. 然后 starts the second half of the sentence.
ex: First I'll eat, then I'll read.
You go first, then I'll go.
我们先去北京，然后去上海。
We'll go to Beijing first, then Shanghai.
gap: First I'll eat, then go to school.
Have your tea first, then we'll leave.
order: First I'll eat, then I'll read.
We'll go to Beijing first, then Shanghai.
我们|先|去|北京|，|然后|去|上海|。
You go first, then I'll go.
spot: First I'll eat, then I'll read.
You go first, then I'll go.

title: 把: doing something to a thing
why: 把 brings the thing to the front, to say what happens to it. The verb can't stand alone at the end: it needs a result, a place, or 了.
mistake: After 把, the verb must say what became of the thing.
ex: I put the book on the table.
gap: I put the book on the table.
order: I put the book on the table.
spot: I put the book on the table.

title: 被: having something done to it
why: 被 puts what the action happened to first, then who did it. It is the reverse of 把, and it often tells of something unwelcome.
mistake: 被, like 把, needs a result: here, 了.
ex: My book was taken by him.
He was seen by the teacher.
gap: My phone was taken by him.
He was seen by the teacher.
order: My book was taken by him.
The apple was eaten by him.
He was seen by the teacher.
spot: The apple was eaten by him.
My book was taken by him.

title: 着: staying that way
why: 着 after a verb says the state carries on: the door stays open. Followed by another verb, it says how the second action is done: sitting and reading.
mistake: 着 says it is still that way, so it doesn't take 了.

title: 地: how, before a verb
why: 地 turns a description into an adverb: 慢慢地 is "slowly". All three de sound alike: 的 goes before a noun, 地 before a verb, and 得 after a verb.
mistake: 地 and its description come before the verb.

title: 如果…就: if, then
why: 如果 sets the condition. 就 goes in the second half, after the subject and right before the verb.
ex: If it rains, I won't go.
If you want to go, we'll go.
If I have time, I'll read.
gap: If it rains tomorrow, I won't go.
If you come, I'll be happy.
如果有时间，我们___去北京。
If we have time, we'll go to Beijing.
order: If it rains, I won't go.
If I have time, I'll read.
If you want to go, we'll go.
spot: If it rains, I won't go.

title: 一…就: as soon as
why: 一 before the first verb and 就 before the second say that the second thing follows straight away.
ex: As soon as I get home, I eat.
He understands as soon as he looks.
She phoned me as soon as she arrived.
gap: As soon as I get home, I eat.
He understands as soon as he looks.
She phoned me as soon as she arrived.
order: As soon as I get home, I eat.
As soon as he arrives, he makes a phone call.
She understands as soon as she looks.
spot: As soon as I get home, I eat.
He understands as soon as he looks.

title: 越来越: more and more
why: 越来越 says something keeps changing, getting more and more so. It already means "more", so 很 can't go with it.
mistake: No 很 after 越来越.
ex: The weather is getting colder and colder.
My Chinese is getting better and better.
Things are getting more and more expensive.
order: Things here are getting more expensive.

title: 又…又: both at once
why: 又…又 says two things are true at the same time, each with its own 又. They are usually both good, or both bad.
ex: This is both cheap and good.
gap: This apple is big and tasty.
order: This is both cheap and good.

title: 除了: besides, or except
pattern: 除了 + A，subject + 也 or 都 + verb
why: The second half decides the meaning. With 也, A is included: "besides A, also". With 都, A is left out: "everyone except A".
ex: Besides tea, I also like coffee.
We are all going, except him.
除了星期天，我每天都工作。
I work every day except Sunday.
gap: Besides tea, I also like coffee.
We are all going, except him.
Besides Chinese, I can also speak English.
order: Besides tea, I also like coffee.
We are all going, except him.
Besides Chinese, I can also speak English.
除了|中文|，|我|也|会|说|英语|。
spot: Besides tea, I also like coffee.
We are all going, except him.
